Author(s): Vivek Gupta, Nitin Chitranshi, Veer Gupta, Yuyi You, Rashi Rajput, Joao A. Paulo, Mehdi Mirzaei, Maarten van den Buuse, Stuart L. Graham

articles.title: Dissection of neuropsychiatric-relevant behavioral and structural phenotypes utilizing neuron type-specific ablation of the Bassoon gene in mice
articles.content: Rare pathogenic mutations in the human BSN gene, which encodes the presynaptic cytomatrix protein Bassoon-a key organizer of the neurotransmitter release apparatus have been linked to neuropsychiatric conditions including schizophrenia. Here we began to dissect the potential contribution of Bsn deficiency in distinct populations of mouse (fore)brain neurons on behavioral and anatomical alterations resembling schizophrenia-like phenotypes. To this end, conditional knockout mice lacking Bassoon in subsets of inhibitory synapses (BsnDlx5/6cKO), in forebrain excitatory synapses (BsnEmx1cKO), or at dopaminergic release sites (BsnDATcKO) were generated. The mice were assessed using prepulse inhibition, a paradigm that models sensorimotor gating, which is often impaired in schizophrenia, and a fear/safety learning paradigm. Further, anxiety-related behaviors were evaluated and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed to assess anatomical brain alterations. Our data reveal synapse-specific effects of the Bassoon deficiency. Sensory gating deficits were observed in both BsnDlx5/6cKO and BsnEmx1cKO mice. BsnDlx5/6cKO mice further demonstrated impaired discrimination between conditioned fear and safety-a condition frequently observed in individuals with schizophrenia. By contrast, BsnDATcKO mice displayed enhanced discrimination between conditioned fear and safety. All mouse strains showed elevated anxiety-like behavior in the light/dark box. Structural MRI revealed increased brain volumes in BsnDlx5/6cKO and BsnEmx1cKO mice, with the most pronounced changes in the hippocampus and cortex. Previous studies have shown that BsnDlx5/6cKO mice display autistic-like behaviors, altered hippocampal network activity and epilepsy. Our findings support the notion that deficits in Bsn-mediated functions, particularly in interneurons, may contribute to the etiology of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions.
articles.author: Kreutzmann, J. C., Angenstein, F., Fejtova, A., Stork, O., Gundelfinger, E. D., Fendt, M., Annamneedi, A.

articles.title: Oral Bacterial Translocation Promotes Lung Dysbiosis and Infection Risk after Spinal Cord Injury
articles.content: Spinal cord injury (SCI) causes systemic pathophysiology that extends beyond the injured spinal cord. Respiratory infections remain a leading cause of death after SCI and can impair neurological recovery, yet the microbial source of these infections remains poorly defined. This study defined the onset and origin of pulmonary dysbiosis after SCI by testing whether commensal bacteria move to the lung from the gut or oral cavity. In a murine model, bacterial culture, 16S rRNA sequencing and source-tracking analyses showed that SCI rapidly increased lung bacterial burden and shifted the pulmonary microbiome toward an oral-like community. Gut-associated bacteria did not measurably reach the lung through lymphatic or vascular routes. Systemic antibiotics commonly used to treat infection failed to reliably reduce post-SCI lung bacterial burden. In contrast, oral and lung-directed antibiotic delivery reduced bacteria linked to post-injury dysbiosis more effectively. These findings identify the oral cavity as a proximal source of lung dysbiosis after SCI, and support route-specific strategies to prevent respiratory infection after SCI.
articles.author: Mifflin, K. A., Kigerl, K. A., Manrique, P., Cyr, A., Medipally, A. K., Guan, Z., Gowdy, K. M., Popovich, P. G.

articles.title: Inter-Individual Variability in Cycling Biomechanics During Experimentally Induced Movement-Evoked Knee Pain
articles.content: Knee pain can alter lower-limb loading and contribute to inter-limb asymmetry, affecting movement mechanics and rehabilitation. Although cycling is frequently prescribed during rehabilitation, the effects of pain on bilateral cycling biomechanics remain poorly understood. This study investigated experimentally induced movement-evoked knee pain on bilateral torque and power output, inter-limb asymmetry, and inter-individual motor responses during cycling. Twenty-three healthy adults (14M and 9F) completed an incremental cycling test followed by eight randomized constant-load trials under pain and no-pain conditions at two intensities. A custom closed-loop torque-dependent electrical stimulation system induced movement-evoked knee pain during the downstroke while bilateral biomechanics were recorded. At higher intensities, movement-evoked knee pain reduced torque (p=0.026, d=0.566) and power (p=0.010, d=0.657) production in the painful limb and altered the normalized symmetry index (NSI) for power (p=0.005, d=0.659), and torque (p<0.001, d=0.754). At lower intensity, pain-leg power (p=0.154) and torque (p=0.104) did not differ significantly between conditions, although torque NSI indicated greater reliance on the non-pain leg (p=0.017, d=0.538). Despite these group-level responses, substantial inter-individual variability was observed ranging from pronounced unloading to increased pain-leg contribution. These findings demonstrate that movement-evoked knee pain alters cycling mechanical output toward the non-painful limb, with substantial heterogeneity in individual motor responses.
articles.author: Sweeney, S., Hosseini, A., Rasoulian, S., Ahmadi, R., Roach, K. E., Park, J., Komeili, A., Aboodarda, S. J.

articles.title: Hypothesis-Driven Identification of Neural Algorithms With Dynamical Structure-Preserving Manifolds.
articles.content: Neuroscience aims to uncover the algorithms by which the brain builds and manipulates rich internal representations of objects, agents, and places. Existing reverse-engineering frameworks remain ineffective for identifying these algorithms. Here, we present Dynamical Structure-Preserving Manifolds (dSPMs)---a novel multilevel reverse-engineering framework that programs, without training, recurrent neural networks to enable hypothesis-driven identification of the brain's algorithms that generate symbolic, structure-preserving representations of the world around. We apply dSPM to identify an algorithm for physical scene prediction in the dorsomedial frontal cortex (DMFC) of macaques intercepting a ball on a Pong-like virtual gameboard. dSPM better explained DMFC than alternatives, made predictions confirmed in neural data, and revealed an algorithm of DMFC that we term 'manifold-based simulation': perceived initial conditions rapidly collapse neural activity onto a low-dimensional manifold whose geometry encodes a physics-based representation of the scene, supporting far-out predictions without traditional next-step simulation. dSPM supports effective exploration of the computational foundations of biological intelligence.
articles.author: Calbick, D., Kim, J. Z., Sohn, H., Yildirim, I.

articles.title: Depth-Dependent Alterations in Cerebral Blood and Tissue Oxygenation Associated with Tau in Alzheimer's Disease Models
articles.content: Vascular dysfunction is an increasingly recognized feature of Alzheimer's disease, and inadequate oxygen delivery may contribute to neuronal death. However, how cerebral oxygenation relates to neuronal pathology remains unclear. Here, we used two-photon phosphorescence lifetime microscopy with Oxyphor2P to measure intravascular and tissue partial pressure of oxygen (pO2) at 0, 100 and 200 um cortical depth in awake rTg4510 and THY-Tau22 mice. Relative to WT, capillary and venular pO2 in rTg4510 mice were elevated at 6 months but reduced at 9 months, mainly in deeper layers, with increased oxygen extraction fraction. Suppressing the tau transgene with doxycycline for three months did not restore vascular pO2. THY-Tau22 mice, despite limited tangle pathology, showed even greater reductions in capillary pO2 at every depth. In 6-month-old rTg4510 mice, tissue pO2 trended lower than in WT, and the fraction of low pO2 values (< 18 mmHg) increased with depth, reaching 33% at 200 um versus 4% in WT. Labeling neurofibrillary tangles with the tau-binding dye HS84 revealed significantly lower tissue pO2 in tangle-positive areas at 100 and 200 um. Longitudinal imaging of 2,282 neurons showed that disappearing neurons were not located in relatively hypoxic tissue within an animal. Finally, ex vivo immunostaining revealed neuronal loss and increased astrogliosis in rTg4510 mice, with unchanged vascular architecture. These results indicate that tau disrupts cerebrovascular and tissue oxygenation in a depth- and age-dependent manner, and that neuronal loss is not explained by a neuron's local oxygen microenvironment but may reflect a global reduction in cortical oxygenation.

articles.title: Supramodal Coding of Detection and Confidence in the Human Cortex
articles.content: Perception is inherently multisensory, yet it remains unclear whether the brain detects stimuli and evaluates confidence in these detections using circuits shared across senses or circuits specific to each modality. Prior evidence is limited: scalp electrophysiology cannot localize where a shared code operates, whereas functional imaging cannot resolve its timing. We recorded intracranial activity (stereoelectroencephalography) in eight patients with epilepsy who performed a near-threshold audiovisual detection task in which they reported, on each trial, whether a visual, auditory, or audiovisual stimulus was present and rated their confidence, both overall and separately for each modality. Analyzing high-gamma activity at the single-channel and region-of-interest levels, we found that stimulus detection involved a broadly distributed, largely supramodal set of cortical regions responding regardless of modality, including the insula, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and superior temporal gyrus. Multivariate decoders trained to distinguish detected from undetected stimuli in one modality generalized to the other modality, indicating a shared detection code within these regions. Confidence relied on a more mixed architecture but was also substantially supramodal. Finally, the auditory cortex encoded confidence information about its non-preferred (visual) modality, with a similar effect in the visual cortex for auditory confidence, suggesting that the involvement of sensory cortices in confidence is not confined to its preferred input.
articles.author: Porte, P., Robin, A., Boscher, F., Dezier, C., Goueytes, D., Mahdian, S., Hoffmann, D., Kahane, P., Minotti, L., Pereira, M., Caron-Guyon, J., Goupil, L., Faivre, N.

articles.title: Adaptive-optics lattice light-sheet microscopy enables correlative single-molecule imaging of endogenous proteins in native environments
articles.content: Resolving molecular organization and dynamics in native environments remains challenging, as single-molecule imaging requires high sensitivity and spatiotemporal resolution while preserving 3D cellular context. Here, we present ALPINE (Adaptive-optics Lattice light-sheet microscopy for endogenous Protein Imaging in Native Environments), a modular framework for quantitative single-molecule imaging into complex biological samples. ALPINE combines adaptive-optics lattice light-sheet microscopy, programmable PSF shaping and acquisition stabilization, an engineered cell-specific labelling toolkit for endogenous cell-surface proteins and analysis pipelines assigning molecular localizations and trajectories to 3D cellular compartments. Labelling endogenous AMPA receptors in intact brain tissue, we demonstrate aberration-corrected 3D single-molecule localization and nanoscale organization within neuronal compartments. Importantly, fast optical sectioning of lattice light-sheet illumination further enables 3D single-molecule tracking in live tissue and quantification of molecular dynamics within native cellular environment. Together, ALPINE provides a modular approach to investigate how endogenous molecules are organized and dynamically regulated in complex biological systems, with components adaptable to diverse biological questions and imaging modalities.

articles.title: The role of urothelial PIEZO ion channels in urinary function
articles.content: The urothelium is increasingly recognized as a dynamic sensory interface that contributes to the regulation of urinary tract function. Mechanosensitive PIEZO ion channels expressed by urothelial cells have been proposed to play important roles in bladder fullness sensation and urinary reflexes. However, the functional contribution of urothelial PIEZO channels to these processes remains unclear. Here, we investigated the consequences of urothelial Piezo1 and Piezo2 deletion using the commonly used Upk2-cre transgenic line. Surprisingly, combined deletion of urothelial PIEZO channels did not alter urinary behavior, and mice lacking urothelial PIEZO1/2 exhibited normal bladder pressure-volume relationships, indicating preserved bladder filling and voiding function. Notably, Upk2-cre; Piezo1fl/fl mice displayed enhanced external urethral sphincter reflex activity during voiding, suggesting that loss of PIEZO1 from cells targeted by Upk2-cre may influence sensory signaling outside of the bladder urothelium. Consistent with this possibility, we identified substantial off-target Cre expression in dorsal root ganglia. These findings demonstrate that the Upk2-cre line is not restricted to the urothelium and therefore raises important considerations for interpreting associated phenotypes attributed specifically to urothelial gene deletion. Biologically, this raises the possibility that PIEZO1 does not influence bladder pressure-volume handling but might contribute to urinary reflexes.
articles.author: Hamed, Y. M. F., Odem, M. A., Pendyala, S., Kwok, T. B., Marshall, K. L.

articles.title: Fiber-Coupled Rotating Two-Photon Light-Sheet Microscopy for Physiological Vestibular Imaging in Larval Zebrafish
articles.content: Physiological vestibular stimulation requires macroscopic rotation of the animal, making simultaneous high-resolution neural imaging technically demanding. Here we present a fiber-coupled rotating two-photon light-sheet microscope for physiological pitch-axis vestibular imaging in larval zebrafish. Two-photon excitation is attractive in this context because near-infrared excitation avoids visible-light contamination of the visual environment. Femtosecond pulses were delivered to the rotating microscope through a broadband hollow-core negative-curvature fiber previously characterized in static light-sheet configurations. The rotating instrument maintained the axial mechanical stability required for cellular-resolution imaging, with submicron mean axial displacement over the characterized angular range. Fiber performance under rotation was also stable: bend-induced transmission changes were small in the relevant curvature regime, and circular input polarization suppressed rotation-dependent polarization artefacts to below 1% in the sample plane. The dominant rotation-sensitive optical limitation was not the fiber but perturbation of the thermal lens in the sample chamber. Reducing fluid motion along the excitation path suppressed this artefact and restored stable imaging during dynamic rotation. With this system, we recorded brain-wide vestibular responses during sinusoidal pitch stimulation and resolved anatomically organized cellular response patterns across the brain. These results establish rotating two-photon light-sheet microscopy as a practical solution for vestibular imaging in experiments that require physiological stimulation together with darkness or controlled visual conditions.

CLSP-REQA: a real-time quality-aware closed-loop seizure prediction framework with Mamba-BiLSTM and confidence-gated intervention
articles.content: IntroductionReliable seizure prediction is a prerequisite for closed-loop neurostimulation therapy, yet existing methods rarely account for the variability in EEG signal quality encountered in real-world deployment, and the overwhelming majority adopt non-strict evaluation protocols that overestimate generalization performance.MethodsWe propose CLSP-REQA (Closed-Loop Seizure Prediction with Real-time EEG Quality Assessment), a unified framework that embeds a lightweight signal quality estimator directly within the prediction pipeline. A Real-time EEG Quality Assessment (REQA) module runs in parallel with a Mamba-BiLSTM backbone, producing a scalar quality score q ∈ [0, 1] that modulates output confidence through a tiered non-linear fusion function (ECLO). We conducted dedicated experiments testing whether this learned score reflects genuine signal quality rather than a redundant proxy for the prediction task, and a sensitivity analysis of the fusion thresholds against standard calibration baselines. The framework was evaluated under strict cross-patient evaluation on the CHB-MIT Scalp EEG Database (n = 23 subjects, 198 seizures) and the SIENA Scalp EEG Database (n = 14 subjects, 47 seizures).ResultsOn CHB-MIT, CLSP-REQA achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.7426 ± 0.0199, exceeding the unadapted cross-patient baseline of 0.69 reported by Jemal et al., using only 16 EEG channels compared to 23 in prior work, and without requiring any target-patient data or domain adaptation. On SIENA, CLSP-REQA achieved an AUC of 0.7012 ± 0.0249, exceeding the best domain-adapted cross-patient result of 0.61 on the same dataset under a strictly harder information constraint, since domain adaptation methods are given access to unlabelled target-patient data that CLSP-REQA does not use.DiscussionThe framework outputs a structured four-tuple 〈p, q, c, ΦSHAP〉 designed for compatibility with closed-loop neurostimulator interfaces. As both evaluation datasets are retrospective recordings from controlled hospital settings, we report this study as a feasibility demonstration rather than evidence of prospective, real-world clinical readiness, and the comparison with domain adaptation should not be read as unconditional superiority.

articles.title: Show HN: Stoke Money – Personal finance app built around a cash flow forecast
articles.content:
Hi HN,

I've been through many finance tracking apps, starting with Personal Capital, then Monarch, and most recently Copilot. None of them have worked perfectly for my needs.

All of these apps tend to model “cash flow” as the net sum of your transactions during a month, yet while credit card charges are reported immediately, they are typically deducted from checking (cash) accounts the following month when the bill is due. As a result, I've always had to maintain a separate spreadsheet to track my actual cash flow.

These apps also have a huge focus on managing budgets, which has never been for me. My spending is rarely consistent month-to-month, so every month I'm comparing my fully justified spending against my budget, and tweaking my budget until I “pass”.

So I built yet another finance tracking app. It has the usual components - accounts, transactions, categories - but the core is a cash flow projection engine, and everything else is built around it.

Budgets are gone. Instead, each income/spending category is projected forward from your historical activity, but not as a flat monthly number. They land in whatever account you historically use (e.g. checking account for paychecks/rent/bills, credit/debit cards for daily spending). Credit card payments are modeled automatically based on your projected credit card balance. You can set up your own recurring transfers between accounts as well, to model savings, for example.

The end result is that the app can forecast how your cash moves, and you can see in advance when any account might run low. If all of your accounts look good for the next 12 months, maybe you don't have a budgeting problem.

What’s made the biggest difference for me has been the MCP integration, which I have connected to Claude (but can be connected to any AI agent of your choice). I have asked it to import historical transactions by uploading PDF account statements, categorize/tag all transactions that took place while I was on vacation, and plan transfers across my accounts to cover expected payments.

I hope some people that share my frustrations will find this app useful.
